_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: There were ten holes in it: and in each hole there was one pipe, and in each and every pipe there were ten holes, and from each hole of a pipe it produced a type of tune. It emerges that the whole of it produced one hundred types of tune.
rashi:a1.2: And your mnemonic: so that you will not err as to who said a hundred and who said a thousand.
rashi:a1.3: A baraita [speaks in] exaggeration: it is the way of mishnayot to teach in exaggeration, such as those [statements] that [the Gemara] cites in [tractate] Ḥullin, in chapter Gid HaNasheh (Ḥullin 90b).
rashi:a3.1: Rabbi Yosei: who said they were Israelites of pure lineage, what does he hold? Rather, everyone [agrees that] the primary component of song is with the mouth.
rashi:a5.1: Both for tithes: for we establish him in the presumptive status of a Levite.
rashi:a7.1: And I have given the Levites: and the Levites are the singers.
rashi:a9.1: That is with the Name: in which they mention the name of Heaven. A person sings song only out of joy and goodness of heart, as it is written: “Behold, My servants shall sing for goodness of heart” (Isaiah 65:14).
rashi:a12.1: But say first fruits: and this is what the verse means: because you did not bring first fruits.
rashi:a13.1: From where [is it derived] that first fruits require song: for they say “I will extol You, Lord, for You have drawn me up” (Psalms 30:2), as we learned in tractate Bikkurim (3:4).
rashi:a13.2: Goodness, goodness: here [with regard to first fruits] it is written “in all the goodness,” and with regard to song it is written (Deuteronomy 28:47): “with joyfulness and with goodness of heart.”
rashi:a15.1: Fruit: with regard to first fruits it is written (Deuteronomy 26:2): “of the first of all the fruit.”
rashi:a15.2: He brought grapes: to the Temple courtyard as first fruits, and pressed them: from where [is it derived] that he has fulfilled [his obligation]? The verse states: “which you shall bring in from your land,” in any case.
rashi:a16.1: (He was master of lifting) Ḥizkiyya said from here: we have found [a source for] the Levites’ song from the Torah. “He was master of lifting [yasor bamassa]”: the lifting of the voice in song.
rashi:a17.1: Balvatei: the name of a sage.
rashi:a17.2: Song: [is the work that] requires the service of an offering, for it is said only over the wine of the offering’s libations, as it is written (Numbers 10:10): “And you shall blow with the trumpets over your burnt offerings.”
rashi:a18.1: They shout from the sea: they will shout in song in the Temple more than the shouting at the Red Sea.
rashi:a19.1: Cites it from here: [the source for] the basic requirement of song from the Torah.
tosafot:a4.1: No, everyone [agrees that] the primary component of song is with the mouth: There is a difficulty. In chapter HeḤalil (Sukka 51a) it says that if the primary component of song is with the mouth, then the song of an offering does not override Shabbat and the festival in order to perform it with an instrument. If so, the mishna [there] that teaches “For twelve days [of the year] the flute plays” — whose view is it? One can say that certainly the tanna’im of our mishna hold that the primary component of song is with the mouth, but there is a tanna there, Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, who says that song with an instrument [for an offering] overrides Shabbat and the festival, and the first clause [of that mishna] accords with him.
tosafot:a6.1: The song is indispensable to the offering: There is a difficulty, for the song is at the time of the libation, and the libation does not hold back the offering, for a person may bring his offering today and the libations from now until four days later (Menaḥot 15b). And it seems [right] to explain that “the song is indispensable to the offering” means [it is indispensable to] the libation: for if there is no song, there is no libation.
tosafot:a11.1: It is called “rejoicing the heart”; it is not called “goodness”: And if you say: But isn’t it written [of Torah]: “For I give you good doctrine” (Proverbs 4:2), and “The Torah of Your mouth is good to me” (Psalms 119:72)? One can say that this is what it means: it is called “rejoicing the heart,” [but] “goodness” placed next to joy, so that its meaning is an expression of joy, it is not called. Alternatively: “goodness” placed next to “heart” it is not called. And if you say: But isn’t it written: “And his heart was merry [vayitav libo]” (Ruth 3:7), and Rashi explained that the midrash has: his heart was merry with Torah study; and likewise we expound in Shabbat (63b) “Let your heart cheer you [vitivkha libkha]” as referring to Torah study? One can say that these are not written explicitly. And according to this [second explanation], the objection “But say first fruits” does not fit well, since they are not called “goodness placed next to heart.” One can say that indeed this is what [the Gemara] answers, that we require goodness placed next to heart. However, since it already knew from the outset that we require goodness placed next to heart, it should not have needed to object again from first fruits. And the first explanation is the main one.
tosafot:a13.1: In brief: From where [is it derived] that first fruits require song: Rashi explains that they required song, as the mishna in Bikkurim (3:4) teaches that the flute played before those bringing them; the Gemara’s challenge “Is that so? But Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani said…” is then a challenge to Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani. Question: why not challenge him directly from that mishna? Answer: the Talmud does not cite the mishna of the order Zera’im, and Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani’s statement is brought only incidentally. Our teacher holds instead, against Rashi, that the song in the Bikkurim mishna is not the essential song but only for joy, which is why the Gemara does not challenge him from it; and it is puzzling [for Rashi], since that mishna does not speak of the essential song at all. Rabbi Elḥanan further asked: how can the Gemara set the Bikkurim mishna in a case of one who brought grapes and pressed them, when it speaks of all first fruits, figs, wheat and all seven species? One cannot explain that the question is whether grapes brought and then pressed keep their sanctity as first fruits, since Ḥullin (120b) teaches that one brings first fruits as liquid only from olives and grapes, so liquid from them clearly counts. One might explain that he set aside grapes and pressed them, and “you shall bring” teaches they are fit; and the baraita that one brings liquid only from olives and grapes would mean after the fact. But the verse is the source for saying song over first fruits, and how would it speak of an after-the-fact case? So Tosafot explain that it speaks of bringing them so from the outset: “you shall bring” teaches that one may bring pressed grapes ab initio, and the Bikkurim mishna fits too, since it speaks of the liquids of olives and grapes, over which song is said from the outset; and once song was instituted over them, it was instituted over all first fruits of the seven species. None of the earlier difficulties remain, and the matter requires examination in the Jerusalem Talmud. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:a16.1: Do not read yasor but yashir: It is puzzling, for there are many verses in Chronicles (I Chronicles 9) [saying] that the sons of so-and-so were singers. One can say that he needs to find that song is from the Torah; therefore he infers it from this verse, where it is written “yasor bamassa” [lifting], and [in the Torah] it is written “the service of bearing [massa]” (Numbers 4:47). Alternatively, he derives from [these] verses that it is a service, so that a non-Levite [lit. stranger] is liable to death for it.
gershom:a1.1: There were ten holes in it: in its handle, which was entirely hollow.
gershom:a2.1: A baraita [speaks in] exaggeration: the external teaching [the baraita] always errs [i.e., overstates].
gershom:a3.1: The primary component of song is with the mouth: the song that the Levites would say with their mouths is the primary component of song.
gershom:a4.1: [And can you understand? Rabbi Yosei, who said they were Israelites, what does he hold? etc.]
gershom:a5.1: One elevates from the platform both to lineage and to tithes: and as for what they saw, that [these men] stood among the Levites, one does not examine whether they played with an instrument or [sang] with the mouth; one elevates [them] to lineage and distributes tithes to them.
gershom:a6.1: One elevates from the platform to lineage: therefore we require [families who may] marry into the priesthood.
gershom:a7.1: But not to tithes: therefore we do not require Levites.
gershom:a8.1: [“To do the service of the children of Israel in the Tent of Meeting,
gershom:a9.1: and to make atonement”]: just as the atonement of the priests, that is, the placing of the blood, is indispensable, so too the service of the Levites, that is, the song, is indispensable.
gershom:a10.1: And the Rabbis: for this [purpose] the service of the Levites is juxtaposed to the atonement of the priests: just as atonement is by day, as it is written “on the day that He commanded” (Leviticus 7:38) [so too song is by day].
gershom:a11.1: [Service] that is with the Name: in which one mentions the Name.
gershom:a12.1: This is song: the mentions [of God’s name] in the psalms; [that is, song, for there are mentions of the Name in the psalms].
gershom:a13.1: But say the lifting of the hands: of the priests, in which there is mention of the Name, since the plain sense of this verse is written about priests, for we derive from it that when a festival falls next to Shabbat, whether before it or after it, all the priestly watches were equal in dividing the shewbread, as it is said: “And if a Levite comes from any of your gates” (Deuteronomy 18:6). What is “your gates”? The time when all Israel enter through one gate. And it is written: “They shall have like portions to eat” (Deuteronomy 18:8).
gershom:a14.1: You must say this is song, as it is written: “My servants shall sing for goodness of heart” (Isaiah 65:14).
gershom:a15.1: It is not called goodness of heart: neither Torah nor first fruits.
gershom:a16.1: It is derived [from] goodness, goodness: it is written with regard to song “and with goodness of heart,” and with regard to first fruits “in all the goodness.”
gershom:a17.1: From where that [the Levites] recite song only over wine: at the time of the wine libation, [as it is said: “And the vine said to them,” etc.].
gershom:a18.1: You can find it: even according to Rabbi Yonatan, that one says song over first fruits.
gershom:a19.1: As Rav Yosef teaches [that they are wine]. [The daf reads “Rabbi Yosei”; Rabbeinu Gershom’s text reads “Rav Yosef.”]
gershom:a20.1: (From where that if) he brought grapes as first fruits to Jerusalem and pressed them before he came to the Temple courtyard, from where [is it derived] that it requires bringing as that wine? The verse states “you shall bring,” to include [it].
gershom:a21.1: Yasor bamassa: it is an expression of authority [serara].
gershom:a23.1: What is service that requires service]: you must say this is song, which the Levites say with the mouth, while others serve them with musical instruments and assist them.
gershom:a24.1: And some say: [work] that requires service, for one recites song only at the time of the service [of the offering].
rashi:b1.1: About matters of voice: that He was commanding him to sing, since Moses was a Levite.
rashi:b2.1: So too they: the Levites, in the service of the altar; and you do not find Levites fit for the service of the altar except in song.
rashi:b2.2: Just as you: the verse is addressed to the priests.
rashi:b3.1: You in theirs: priests who entered into the service of the Levites, for example, that they sang.
rashi:b3.2: And they in yours: a Levite who served at the altar like a priest.
rashi:b3.3: They in theirs: for example, a Levite singer who closed the doors, or a Levite gatekeeper who sang song, for the Levites were divided, this one to be a gatekeeper and that one to be a singer.
rashi:b3.4: But only with a prohibition: [its source] has not been explained to us.
rashi:b4.1: Abaye: does not hold of this baraita taught above, “they in theirs are not [liable] to death,” since he finds another tanna who holds as he does.
rashi:b4.2: An actual stranger: for example, an Israelite.
rashi:b4.3: Isn’t it written once: in that very passage itself, and it too refers to the service of the Levites.
rashi:b6.1: Rabbi Yehoshua and Yoḥanan ben Gudgeda were Levites. Yoḥanan ben Gudgeda holds that a singer who served as a gatekeeper is [liable] to death when he closes [the doors] by himself, and the Rabbis decreed against one who assists, lest he come to do it by himself. And Rabbi Yehoshua holds that even when he does it by himself it is only a prohibition, and the Rabbis did not decree against one who assists.
rashi:b9.1: A communal voluntary burnt offering: such as the “dessert of the altar” [kayitz hamizbe’aḥ], which comes from the horn-shaped collection boxes into which they put the money left over from sin offerings and the money left over from guilt offerings.
rashi:b9.2: Your burnt offerings: “And you shall blow with the trumpets over your burnt offerings” (Numbers 10:10), and this is [the source for] song.
rashi:b10.1: And Hezekiah commanded [lit. said]: this implies that he was consulted.
rashi:b10.2: Rather, is it not a voluntary offering: and he was consulted whether they should sing; and it is written “the song of the Lord began,” [meaning] that the court instructed him to have them sing.
rashi:b11.1: The burnt offering of the New Moon: which was an additional offering.
rashi:b13.1: The lamb that comes with the omer: which is an obligatory burnt offering on the sixteenth of Nisan.
rashi:b15.1: Rather, Rav Ashi said: this consulting was not because they were in doubt, for certainly the New Moon had been established in its time; rather, he was taking permission.
rashi:b15.2: Just as with a prayer leader who consults: and takes permission whether he should pray.
rashi:b15.3: You may even say an obligatory burnt offering: it was the daily burnt offering of each and every day.
rashi:b16.1: Merit on an auspicious day: in Nisan they were redeemed, and in Nisan they will be redeemed in the future.
rashi:b17.1: The conclusion of Shabbat: Sunday [lit. the first day of the week].
rashi:b17.2: And the conclusion of the Sabbatical Year: the eighth year.
rashi:b17.3: And He brought upon them their own iniquity: it is a verse in Psalms, in the psalm “God of vengeance, Lord” (Psalms 94).
rashi:b18.1: The daily offering ceased: for they had no lambs, because [the enemy] were besieging Jerusalem and no one could go out or come in.
rashi:b19.1: And what is different about a voluntary burnt offering, that it was [sacrificed]: weren’t lambs unavailable?
rashi:b19.2: That is not difficult; a young bull merely happened to come to them: which is not fit for the daily offering but is fit for a voluntary burnt offering.
rashi:b20.1: And can you understand: that that song was a full song over an offering? But the song of Sunday is “The earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof,” as it says in Rosh HaShana (31a), and this verse is in the psalm “God of vengeance, Lord,” which is the song of Wednesday [lit. the fourth day of the week].
rashi:b20.2: Eiliyya: a lamentation, as the Targum renders “and take up a lamentation on the high hills” (Jeremiah 7:29) with the word eiliyya.
rashi:b21.1: The platform [dukhan] was a kind of bench.
rashi:b21.2: If so: that one recites song even when it is not over an offering, let him also recite it for a voluntary burnt offering, and you would resolve Rabbi Avin’s dilemma.
rashi:b21.3: It would result in a mishap: for this [song] of Reish Lakish is optional, and if one sang for a voluntary burnt offering as an option, people would come to say that [song for] an obligatory burnt offering is also optional. Therefore we do not recite song at all for a voluntary offering.
rashi:b22.1: What came of it: of Rabbi Avin’s dilemma.
rashi:b22.2: And you shall blow with the trumpets over your burnt offerings and over the sacrifices of your peace offerings: it juxtaposes the burnt offering to peace offerings, and peace offerings to the burnt offering, with regard to song.
rashi:b23.1: Just as the burnt offering stated here is of the most sacred order — for you have no burnt offering of lesser sanctity — so too the peace offerings stated here as requiring song: [the verse] speaks of peace offerings of the most sacred order, and you have no peace offerings of the most sacred order except the lambs of Atzeret [Shavuot], which are communal peace offerings, and of them it is written: “They shall be holy to the Lord for the priest” (Leviticus 23:20). And just as the peace offerings stated here with regard to song have a set time, since we have established them as the lambs of Atzeret, so too the burnt offering stated here is one that has a set time, to exclude a communal voluntary offering, which has no set time.
tosafot:b1.1: From here: “It came to pass, when the trumpeters [and singers] were as one”: and in the verse (Numbers 10:10) it is written: “And you shall blow with the trumpets over your burnt offerings.” Evidently there is song [from the Torah].
tosafot:b5.1: A gatekeeper who sang: for in Chronicles (I Chronicles 9) it is written that there were families who were gatekeepers and families who were singers.
tosafot:b5.2: Raises an objection: Rashi explained: I do not know where this prohibition comes from. And Rabbeinu Menaḥem, may his soul rest in Eden, explained: for it is written: “to keep the charge, but he shall do no service” (Numbers 8:26), and it is written there: “Thus shall you do to the Levites with regard to their charges.”
tosafot:b7.1: For one Sage holds it is [liable] to death: if he serves as a gatekeeper by himself, and the Rabbis decreed concerning one who assists another; and one Sage holds it is a prohibition, and the Rabbis did not decree if he comes to assist.
tosafot:b9.1: Does a communal voluntary burnt offering require song: such as the “dessert” burnt offering [of the altar]; but of an individual, even his obligatory offering does not require libations [so the printed text].
tosafot:b13.1: Rather, Rami son of Rav Yeiva said: they were asking about the lamb that comes with the omer: This is very puzzling. What was he thinking? For the day before they had offered the daily offerings and the additional offerings; why did they consult only about the additional offering of the sixteenth of Nisan?
tosafot:b13.2: They were asking whether the New Moon was established: And there is a difficulty for Rashi, for in Chronicles this verse is written before “And the king took counsel… to perform the Passover in the second month” (II Chronicles 30:2).
tosafot:b15.1: Rather, Rav (Shimi) [Ashi] said: just as with a prayer leader who consults: and in truth you cannot resolve [the dilemma from here], for we may say that it was the lamb that comes with the omer.
tosafot:b20.1: The song of the day is “The earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof” (Psalms 24:1): and if the “dessert” burnt offering requires song, it would be the song that they said with the morning daily offering on that day.
tosafot:b21.1: If so, for a voluntary burnt offering: the Kuntres [Rashi] explains: and you would resolve Rabbi Avin’s dilemma.
tosafot:b22.1: “Your burnt offerings and the sacrifices of your peace offerings”: just as the burnt offering is of the most sacred order, so too peace offerings, etc.; and just as peace offerings have a set time, etc.: This baraita is found also in Zevaḥim, in chapter Eizehu Mekoman (Zevaḥim 55a), and it is taught there thus: Just as the burnt offering is of the most sacred order, so too peace offerings are of the most sacred order; just as the burnt offering requires [slaughter in] the north, so too peace offerings, etc. And it does not have there “and just as peace offerings have a set time, etc.,” as it is here. Perhaps all of it — that they require the north and that they have a set time — is one baraita, and Rav Mari taught it thus [here], while there [the Gemara] taught only what it needed of it. Alternatively, the baraita contains only “the burnt offering is of the most sacred order, so too peace offerings are of the most sacred order,” and [the Gemara] draws the further comparisons, with regard to a set time [here] and with regard to requiring the north in Zevaḥim. [So] Rabbeinu Elḥanan.
gershom:b1.1: About matters of voice: when Moses, who was a Levite, would sing, God would answer him with a voice.
gershom:b2.1: So too they in the service of the altar: song at the time of the offering.
gershom:b3.1: You in theirs: that is, if they switched their service, a Levite for a priest, they are [liable] to death.
gershom:b4.1: They in theirs: that is, they switched their service, for example a gatekeeper who sang or a singer who served as a gatekeeper; it is only a warning, a negative prohibition.
gershom:b5.1: Isn’t it written once: “And you shall appoint Aaron and his sons, and they shall keep their priesthood; and the stranger that draws near shall be put to death” (Numbers 3:10). A gatekeeper is the guard of the gates, as it is written: “and watches over the gates.” [We could not locate this last phrase as a verse.]
gershom:b6.1: Rabbi Yehoshua son of Rabbi Ḥanina and Yoḥanan ben Gudgeda were Levites. [So Rabbeinu Gershom’s text; the daf reads “bar Ḥananya.”]
gershom:b7.1: For one Sage holds: Yoḥanan ben Gudgeda, that they are [liable] to death, and the Rabbis decreed that one should not assist, lest he serve as a gatekeeper [by himself], which is [liable] to death.
gershom:b8.1: And one Sage holds: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya, that it is only a prohibition; since there is no sin of death in it, and he only wants to assist him and not actually do it, [the Rabbis did not decree].
gershom:b10.1: A communal voluntary burnt offering: when a miracle was done for them and they volunteered to bring a burnt offering. (For an individual’s voluntary burnt offering, which is frequent, certainly
gershom:b11.1: does not require [song], it seems to me.) An individual’s voluntary burnt offering, which is frequent, certainly requires song [corrected in brackets to: does not require song, it seems to me].
gershom:b12.1: Or perhaps when it says “And you shall blow [with the trumpets] over your burnt offerings,” which is [song],
gershom:b13.1: “your burnt offerings” speaks of all Israel.) [The editor notes:] It seems it should read: “your burnt offerings” speaks of all Israel, and that is the daily burnt offering, which belongs to all Israel; but a voluntary burnt offering is in the category of an individual’s burnt offering and does not require song. [The question is whether it means] a voluntary burnt offering of an (Israel) [individual], or the daily burnt offering, which belongs to all Israel.
gershom:b14.1: And Hezekiah commanded [to offer the burnt offering, etc.]: even though this verse is written about the bull [brought by] the court for idol worship, there are also, there, seven lambs that were not for idol worship. If we say [it was] an obligatory burnt offering, of the daily offering,
gershom:b15.1: why did he need to consult Hezekiah, as it says “And Hezekiah commanded”? [Surely] they knew that it requires song.
gershom:b16.1: On the sixteenth day [of the first month]: evidently it is not the New Moon.
gershom:b17.1: The lamb that comes with the omer: [which is offered on the sixteenth of Nisan, if the New Moon was established in its time, so that the omer would be offered on the sixteenth]. And why did they need to ask? Let them see how they performed the Paschal offering on the fourteenth and how they ate matza, for certainly they would not have done so unless they knew that it had been established in its time.
gershom:b18.1: Rather: in truth they knew that it had been established in its time, and it was the lamb that comes with the omer; and as for what you said, why did they need to consult [him]:
gershom:b19.1: Just as with a prayer leader [who consults], who takes permission before [he stands] to pray, out of respect for the congregation; so too these took permission from him out of respect for the king. And there is a puzzle in this: how can he say that they offered the omer on the sixteenth of Nisan, when Hezekiah intercalated Nisan in Nisan, as is explained [in Chronicles]?
gershom:b20.1: That day was the Ninth of Av: that is, an inauspicious day, the same day on which the congregation wept, as it is written: “And all the congregation lifted up [their voice]” (Numbers 14:1).
gershom:b21.1: And likewise in the second: when the Temple was destroyed the second time, it was the conclusion of Shabbat and the conclusion of the Sabbatical Year.
gershom:b22.1: The daily offering ceased: for they had no more animals to offer.
gershom:b23.1: [That happened to come to them: that they found an animal and offered it as a voluntary burnt offering.
gershom:b24.1: And can you understand: that it was specifically song [over an offering]? But the song of the day said on the first day, that is, at the conclusion of Shabbat, is “The earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof”; “And He brought upon them their own iniquity” is the song of Wednesday, for it is written at the end of the psalm “God of vengeance,” which is said on the fourth day. Rather, they did not say it as an actual song.
gershom:b25.1: Rather, merely a lamentation: a lament that happened to come into their mouths.
gershom:b26.1: But it teaches “standing on their platform,” which implies that they went there for this purpose, to say song; and for a voluntary burnt offering they would not all go up there.
gershom:b27.1: Rather, he holds like Reish Lakish, who says one recites song not over an offering, even though they are not obligated when there are no daily offerings.
gershom:b28.1: (For a voluntary burnt offering also) [For an individual’s burnt offering] also let them say it, even though they are not obligated.
gershom:b29.1: It would result in a mishap: for they would say: Learn from this that a voluntary burnt offering cannot be offered without song; [and sometimes there are no Levites, as when Ezra went up, and they would think that it cannot be offered without song,] and they would not bring it, though it does not require song.
gershom:b30.1: And some say: it would result in a mishap, for they would say: just as with a voluntary burnt offering one may say [song] if he wishes and not say it if he wishes, so too with this obligatory burnt offering, one may say it if he wishes and not say it if he wishes.
gershom:b31.1: Come and hear: “And you shall blow with the trumpets over your burnt offerings and over the sacrifices of your peace offerings”: just as the burnt offering [which is of the most sacred order requires song and trumpets, so too peace offerings of the most sacred order, that is, the two lambs of Atzeret, which are peace offerings and are eaten only by a priest, like the sin offering and the guilt offering, which are of the most sacred order, as it is written: “They shall be holy to the Lord for the priest”] have a set time: on Atzeret.
gershom:b32.1: So too a burnt offering that has a set time: that is, all obligatory burnt offerings; and from here [the verse] excludes a voluntary burnt offering.
